intro.speaker: mira
intro.text: New case: a 2004 paper claims one simple model — Map and Reduce — can run huge jobs across thousands of machines.

intro.speaker: summary
intro.text: Two functions, one model, every job. I skimmed the abstract, that's basically the whole paper.

intro.speaker: mira
intro.text: Let's see if your 'skim' holds up once we look at what Map and Reduce actually do.

boss.mechanicReason: Frame boss: test whether the suspect's claims about the model and examples hold up against the paper.

item.speaker: summary
item.prompt: The Summary's version of the Map/Reduce model and its examples. One claim overgeneralizes - present the passage that disproves it.

statements.text: Map takes an input pair and produces a set of intermediate key/value pairs.
statements.why: This is exactly how the paper defines the Map function.

sourceRefs.quote: Map, written by the user, takes an input pair and pro- duces a set of intermediate key/value pairs.

statements.text: Reduce receives the grouped values for a key through an iterator, which lets it handle lists too large to fit in memory.
statements.why: The paper explicitly describes the iterator and its purpose.

sourceRefs.quote: The intermediate val- ues are supplied to the user’s reduce function via an iter- ator.

statements.text: In the Distributed Grep example, the reduce function just copies the matched data straight to the output.
statements.why: This is stated directly as the identity behavior of grep's reduce step.

sourceRefs.quote: The reduce function is an identity function that just copies the supplied intermedi- ate data to the output.

statements.text: Since grep's reduce just copies data, every reduce function in these examples really just copies data to the output.
statements.why: This generalizes from one example (grep) to all of them, but the URL counting, link-graph, and term-vector examples all show reduce aggregating or merging values, not copying them.

sourceRefs.quote: The reduce function adds together all values for the same URL and emits a 〈URL,total count〉 pair.

hints: Which claim takes one example's behavior and stretches it to cover every example?

outro.speaker: mira
outro.text: Case closed. Map and Reduce are real, but 'identity' only describes grep — the other examples merge or total up data.

intro.speaker: mira
intro.text: Second case: the paper reports real timing numbers from grep and sort runs at Google, plus a list of production uses.

intro.speaker: summary
intro.text: Numbers, numbers. I don't need the graphs, I already know the gist.

intro.speaker: mira
intro.text: The gist is exactly where people cut corners. Let's check your timeline against the paper's.

boss.mechanicReason: Frame boss: pressure-test the suspect's performance claims against the measured results.

item.speaker: summary
item.prompt: The Summary's recap of the performance experiments. One claim confuses a milestone with the whole job finishing - present the passage that corrects it.

statements.text: Disabling backup tasks made the sort job take 44% longer to finish.
statements.why: The paper reports exactly this increase when backup tasks are turned off.

sourceRefs.quote: The entire computation takes 1283 seconds, an increase of 44% in elapsed time.

statements.text: Google's sort run finished in less time than the best reported TeraSort benchmark result.
statements.why: 891 seconds for the MapReduce sort is directly compared to the 1057-second TeraSort figure.

sourceRefs.quote: This is similar to the current best reported result of 1057 seconds for the TeraSort benchmark [18].

statements.text: When a task is lagging near the end of a job, the master schedules a backup execution rather than waiting on the slow machine.
statements.why: This is the described straggler-mitigation mechanism.

sourceRefs.quote: When a MapReduce operation is close to completion, the master schedules backup executions of the remaining in-progress tasks.

statements.text: Since the grep job's transfer rate hit zero at about 80 seconds, the whole computation was done by then too.
statements.why: The rate hitting zero only marks the end of map work; the paper states the entire computation, including startup overhead, took about 150 seconds.

sourceRefs.quote: The entire computation takes approximately 150 seconds from start to finish.

hints: Compare the moment a rate hits zero to the total time the paper reports for the whole job.

outro.speaker: mira
outro.text: Case closed. The sort numbers and the backup-task logic check out — but 'rate hits zero' isn't the same as 'job done'.
